chapter: Left out of the jazz books; Tatum, Handy and family
title: His grandmother Mary Jane Gorham: slavery, a plantation piano and a hostile film reaction
summary: Collins's grandmother was sold as a girl, learned piano by watching her mistress's daughter, and a slave film left him angry as it matched her stories.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: In going back through our tapes so far, there are a few things I wanted to ask you. You mentioned your grandmother, and she was a very good pianist.
You know, I tell you, I went to see a movie -- she was a great woman, you know, she was a very fine singer, also. I went to see a movie, the sneak preview

of a movie called "Mandango" or something. Have you heard of this book? But any way, it's about slaves. And the treatment of slaves, and how the white man handled the slaves after that they were brought over here. And my grandmother was a slave as a little girl, and I was very hostile when I came out of this movie because everything she had told me I saw in this movie.

And how they separated families, they separated children from their mothers. And sent -- sold them to other plantation owners. And my grandmother was born in Georgia, and how they sold her to someone in Alabama, and she never saw her mother, any of her relatives any more. when she was sold?

Oh, she was just a little girl. You I don't know. But how she -- the master's daughter, who's taking piano lessons, and she was what they called the house nigger, I guess, you know, she was her companion. And she would be right there when she was taking these lessons, and she learned to read and to play piano by watching her -- this little girl, her mistress, I guess, mistress' daughter, take piano lessons. And my grandmother really had the talent, you know, so she developed from there.
But I saw this movie and it just was -- it just tore me up. But here we go again. From there came your rhythms,

you know, the African rhythms, because as we all know, the Africans are very musical and very rhythmic. Yeah. So it was just ironic that I should go and hear and see this movie and all of this flashed back to me. I think half of the people in there, most of the people in there were hostile when they came out. You know, but musically this is how my grandmother started playing.
So she taught music, as I told you, also, and so did my mother. But my mother was quite talented also.
